sentences.text: Cruralispennia multidonta is an extinct genus of enantiornithine bird, with a name translating to "shin feather" and "many-toothed" respectively.
The holotype specimen — the specific fossil the species is based on — consists of a semi-articulated partial skeleton encased in carbonized feathers.
This bird is distinguished from other members of its group by possessing fourteen teeth in the lower jaw, a notably high count for enantiornitheans.
The upper jaw, or premaxilla, is short and forms a forty-three degree angle with the frontal bone while preserving two teeth.
Its forelimb was short and featured a robust humerus, a structural trait typical of the Enantiornithes.
The toes ended in sharp, curved claws designed for gripping.
A short, broad pygostyle tapers into an upturned tip; this plow-shaped feature is generally associated with more derived birds in the Ornithuromorpha group.
The breastbone, or sternum, displays a V-shaped posterior margin and contains two pairs of internal struts known as trabeculae.
The unique wire-like leg feathers, termed PWFDT, are currently known only in this genus and were also found on the front edge of the left wing.
Analysis of melanosomes in these leg feathers indicates a dark brown coloration due to their shortest aspect ratio.
The early appearance of this derived genus suggests the evolutionary history of ornithothoraces is older than previously indicated by fossils.
The genus was formally described by Wang and colleagues in 2017.
The single known specimen, cataloged as IVPP 21711, was found in the Huajiying Formation of Hebei province, China, and is now housed at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology.
A histological study of the humerus found no lines of arrested growth, indicating the individual died within a single season and reached adult size in less than one year.
This rapid growth strategy contrasts with other enantiornithines, which are believed to have taken several years to reach adulthood.
Researchers suggest that the crural PWFDT feathers may have functioned in insulation, heat shielding, or social signaling.
The narrow crural PWFDT feathers were likely too simple for aerodynamic use but narrow enough not to hinder flight.
Cruralispennia is classified within Enantiornithes based on humerus features, the lack of procoracoid processes, and a long scapular acromion.

Cruralispennia lived during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically the Barremian stage, approximately 130.7 million years ago, within the Hauterivian stage range of 132.6 to 125.77 million years ago.
It is debated whether the unique leg feathers are a novel type or simply immature feathers formed after a recent molt.
It is debated whether the early diversification of enantiornithines seen in Cruralispennia reflects a high evolutionary rate or is an artifact of poor sampling immediately after the Jurassic.
